title: Neoplasms of the Urinary Tract
subject: Renal and Urinary System (RENL)
author: Dr. Sharilyn Rennie

overview.intro: This chapter covers the tumors of the kidney and urinary tract: clear cell renal cell carcinoma and its presentations, the other renal epithelial tumors, Wilms tumor in children, and the urothelial, squamous, and glandular carcinomas of the bladder and collecting system. Each tumor is explained from its cell of origin and its genetic lesion, because those two facts predict the gross and microscopic appearance, the hormones the tumor makes, and the way it spreads. Board questions usually give an age, an exposure, a laboratory abnormality, or a histologic description and ask you to name the tumor or the mechanism behind a finding.
prerequisites: Histology of the nephron and collecting duct, including proximal tubule and intercalated cells, and of the urothelium
Tumor suppressor genes, oncogenes, the two-hit model, and genomic imprinting
Endocrine functions of the kidney (erythropoietin, renin) and the regulation of plasma calcium by PTH
Venous drainage of the kidneys and gonads into the renal veins and inferior vena cava
Embryology of the metanephros, cloaca, allantois, and ventral body wall

connections.how: Von Hippel-Lindau disease, tuberous sclerosis, and hereditary papillary renal cancer show how germline mutations create multiple, bilateral, early-onset renal tumors.
Renal cell carcinoma growing into the renal vein is a cause of renal vein thrombosis and of a left varicocele.
Paraneoplastic erythropoietin, PTHrP, renin, and ACTH explain polycythemia, hypercalcemia, hypertension, and Cushing syndrome in renal cell carcinoma.
Chronic Schistosoma haematobium infection of the bladder wall is the leading cause of bladder squamous cell carcinoma worldwide.

connections.to: Pediatric tumors and neural crest derivatives
connections.how: Wilms tumor must be separated from neuroblastoma, the other common abdominal mass of early childhood.

terms.def: A malignant tumor arising from renal tubular epithelium, the most common primary kidney cancer in adults.
A tumor suppressor on chromosome 3p whose protein targets hypoxia-inducible factor for destruction when oxygen is present.
A transcription factor that switches on genes for angiogenesis, glycolysis, and erythropoietin when cells sense low oxygen.
Signs and symptoms caused by substances a tumor secretes rather than by local growth or metastasis.
A column of tumor tissue growing within the lumen of a vein, as renal cell carcinoma does in the renal vein and inferior vena cava.
A large epithelial cell with granular pink cytoplasm caused by a great excess of mitochondria.
A focus of persistent embryonic metanephric tissue in the postnatal kidney that can give rise to Wilms tumor.
The combination of blastemal, stromal, and epithelial elements that characterizes Wilms tumor.
The transitional epithelium lining the renal pelvis, ureters, bladder, and proximal urethra.
Carcinogenic injury of a whole epithelial surface, so that tumors arise at several sites and recur at new ones.

terms.term: Carcinoma in situ (CIS) of the bladder
terms.def: A flat, high grade urothelial neoplasm confined to the epithelium that has a high risk of invasion.
The fibrous remnant of the allantois that runs from the bladder dome to the umbilicus as the median umbilical ligament.

sections.title: Clear cell renal cell carcinoma: origin, genetics, morphology, and venous spread

blocks.text: Renal cell carcinoma (RCC) accounts for about 85 to 90% of primary malignant kidney tumors in adults. It peaks in the sixth and seventh decades and is about twice as common in men. The clear cell type makes up about 70 to 80% of cases and arises from the epithelium of the proximal tubule, so it usually forms a solitary cortical mass, often at one pole.
Molecular mechanism: pseudohypoxia from VHL loss

The VHL tumor suppressor gene lies on chromosome 3p25. Its protein is the substrate-recognition part of an E3 ubiquitin ligase. When oxygen is present, prolyl hydroxylases use O2 to hydroxylate HIF-alpha, VHL binds the hydroxylated HIF-alpha, and it is destroyed in the proteasome. Most sporadic clear cell tumors lose both VHL copies, typically by deletion of 3p plus mutation or promoter methylation of the remaining allele. HIF-alpha then accumulates even in well oxygenated cells, pairs with HIF-beta, and drives the genes a hypoxic cell would use. In von Hippel-Lindau disease one defective allele is inherited, so only one further hit is needed and tumors are multiple, bilateral, and appear at a younger age.

blocks.title: From VHL loss to a vascular, invasive tumor
steps: Both VHL alleles inactivated in a proximal tubule cell
HIF-alpha escapes ubiquitination and proteasomal degradation
HIF activates VEGF, PDGF, TGF-alpha, GLUT1, and erythropoietin genes
Angiogenesis, growth signaling, and glycolytic metabolism
Highly vascular tumor that invades the renal vein
blocks.caption: Loss of VHL makes the cell behave as if it were hypoxic, which explains the dense vasculature and the growth drive.

blocks.text: Gross and microscopic appearance

The cut surface is golden yellow because the cells store lipid, mottled with gray-white fibrous areas, red-brown hemorrhage, soft necrosis, and cysts. Microscopically, round to polygonal cells have abundant clear cytoplasm, because lipid and glycogen dissolve during tissue processing and leave empty-looking cells. The cells sit in nests and sheets separated by a delicate branching network of thin-walled vessels, the morphologic signature of HIF-driven VEGF, which also explains the frequent hemorrhage. Higher grade tumors show larger nuclei with prominent nucleoli, and sarcomatoid change carries the worst prognosis.

blocks.title: Risk factors for renal cell carcinoma
rows: Strongest modifiable risk factor; risk roughly doubles
Proposed mechanisms include insulin and IGF-1 signaling, adipokines, and lipid peroxidation
Independent association; the mechanism is not settled
Cysts that form in end-stage kidneys during long-term dialysis develop renal carcinomas far more often than normal kidneys
Germline VHL mutation; bilateral multifocal clear cell RCC with cerebellar and retinal hemangioblastomas and pheochromocytoma
Cadmium and trichloroethylene exposure; tuberous sclerosis
blocks.caption: Smoking, obesity, and hypertension drive most sporadic risk; dialysis cysts and VHL disease are special settings.

blocks.text: Venous invasion and spread

Clear cell carcinoma has a strong tendency to grow into the renal vein as a solid tumor thrombus, which can extend up the inferior vena cava and occasionally into the right atrium. This venous route explains why metastasis is mainly hematogenous: tumor fragments carried in caval blood pass through the right heart and lodge first in the pulmonary capillary bed, so the lung is the most common metastatic site, followed by bone. Regional lymph nodes, adrenal, liver, and brain are also involved.

blocks.predict: Why might a patient with clear cell RCC have a hematocrit above the reference range even though arterial oxygen saturation is normal?
blocks.explain: The erythropoietin gene is a HIF target. With VHL lost, HIF stays active in tumor cells regardless of oxygen, so the tumor secretes erythropoietin and drives red cell production without any true hypoxia.

sections.title: Presentations of renal cell carcinoma: local signs, paraneoplastic hormones, and metastasis

blocks.text: The kidney lies deep in the retroperitoneum, surrounded by perirenal fat, so a tumor can grow large before it causes symptoms. Many renal cell carcinomas are now discovered incidentally on imaging done for another reason. When local signs appear, hematuria is the most common, because the tumor erodes into the calyces and pelvis; it may be gross or microscopic and is often intermittent. Flank pain comes from stretching of the renal capsule, hemorrhage into the tumor, or clots passing down the ureter, and a palpable flank mass means the tumor is already large. The classic triad of hematuria, flank pain, and mass occurs together in only about 10% of patients.

Systemic features include fever, weight loss, fatigue, and anemia, which is more common than polycythemia. Renal cell carcinoma is known for paraneoplastic syndromes, partly because HIF drives the erythropoietin gene directly and partly because tumor cells secrete hormones ectopically.

blocks.title: Paraneoplastic products of renal cell carcinoma
rows: Secondary polycythemia with high erythropoietin and normal arterial O2 saturation
Binds the PTH1 receptor on bone and kidney, increasing bone resorption and distal Ca2+ reabsorption
Hypercalcemia with suppressed PTH and often low phosphate
Tumor secretion activates angiotensin II and aldosterone
Ectopic secretion stimulates adrenal cortisol production
Cushing syndrome with hypokalemia and hyperglycemia
blocks.caption: Erythropoietin and renin exaggerate normal renal products; PTHrP and ACTH are ectopic.

blocks.title: Two abnormal laboratory values in one patient
blocks.text: A 64-year-old man who smokes has hematocrit 57% (men about 41 to 50%), arterial O2 saturation 98%, serum calcium 12.4 mg/dL (about 8.5 to 10.5), and PTH below the reference range. Normal saturation rules out hypoxic polycythemia, so the red cell excess is driven by inappropriate erythropoietin. A high calcium with low PTH means the parathyroids are responding normally and something else is raising calcium: PTHrP or osteolytic bone metastasis. A single renal cell carcinoma secreting erythropoietin and PTHrP explains both findings.
Metastasis

About one quarter of patients have metastases when the tumor is found, sometimes before any local symptom. Because spread follows the venous route described in C01, the lung is involved most often, classically as multiple round nodules sometimes called cannonball metastases. Bone metastases are lytic, so they cause pain, pathologic fracture, and a second mechanism of hypercalcemia.
The left varicocele

The left gonadal vein drains into the left renal vein, while the right gonadal vein enters the inferior vena cava directly. Tumor thrombus in the left renal vein therefore blocks outflow from the left pampiniform plexus. A varicocele produced this way does not empty when the patient lies down, unlike the common idiopathic varicocele, which fills with standing and decompresses when supine.

blocks.title: How a left renal tumor produces a left varicocele
steps: Tumor thrombus grows into the left renal vein
Left gonadal vein cannot drain into the renal vein
Pressure rises in the left pampiniform plexus
Varicocele that persists when the patient is supine
blocks.caption: A new varicocele that does not decompress lying down points to an obstructing lesion upstream.

sections.title: Papillary and chromophobe carcinoma and oncocytoma

blocks.text: Renal epithelial tumors are classified by the cell they resemble and the genetic change that drives them. Clear cell and papillary carcinomas come from the proximal tubule, while chromophobe carcinoma and oncocytoma come from intercalated cells of the collecting duct. These origins explain why the tumors look different and why they behave differently.

blocks.title: Renal epithelial tumors compared
rows: Golden yellow; clear cells; delicate vessels
Trisomy 7 and 17; MET in hereditary cases
Papillae with foamy macrophages in fibrovascular cores
Pale cells, distinct cell borders, perinuclear halo
Mahogany brown; central stellate scar; mitochondria-rich pink cells
blocks.caption: Origin pairs the tumors: proximal tubule for clear cell and papillary, intercalated cell for chromophobe and oncocytoma.

blocks.text: Papillary carcinoma

Papillary carcinoma is the second most common subtype. Its characteristic cytogenetic changes are trisomy of chromosomes 7 and 17, often with loss of Y in men, and it does not depend on VHL loss. Hereditary papillary renal carcinoma is caused by activating germline mutations of MET on 7q, which encodes the receptor tyrosine kinase for hepatocyte growth factor; extra copies of chromosome 7 increase the dose of the same growth signal in sporadic tumors. Microscopically, tumor cells cover papillae built on fibrovascular cores, and the cores often contain foamy, lipid-laden macrophages and sometimes psammoma bodies. These tumors are frequently multifocal and bilateral and are common in kidneys with dialysis-associated cystic disease.
Chromophobe carcinoma and oncocytoma

Chromophobe carcinoma arises from intercalated cells and shows extensive loss of whole chromosomes, leaving a markedly hypodiploid genome. Its cells have pale to eosinophilic cytoplasm, prominent plant-like cell membranes, and a clear halo around the nucleus. It has a better prognosis than clear cell or papillary carcinoma.

Oncocytoma is a benign epithelial tumor that also comes from intercalated cells. Its cells are oncocytes, packed so densely with mitochondria that the cytoplasm is granular and pink, and the abundant mitochondria give the tumor its tan to mahogany-brown color. A central stellate scar is typical. Because chromophobe carcinoma and oncocytoma share an origin and both can look eosinophilic, they are separated by the distinct membranes and perinuclear halos of chromophobe cells and by the round, uniform nuclei of oncocytes. Birt-Hogg-Dube syndrome (FLCN mutation) produces both tumor types, sometimes as hybrid tumors.

blocks.predict: A renal mass is composed of granular eosinophilic cells. Which findings would push you toward oncocytoma rather than chromophobe carcinoma?
blocks.explain: Uniform round nuclei without perinuclear halos, no prominent cell membranes, a brown cut surface with a central stellate scar, and no loss of multiple whole chromosomes favor oncocytoma, the benign mitochondria-rich tumor.

blocks.text: Wilms tumor is the most common primary renal tumor of childhood, with most cases diagnosed between 2 and 5 years of age. It arises from metanephric blastema, the embryonic tissue that normally forms nephrons. Its precursor lesions are nephrogenic rests, foci of metanephric tissue that persist after birth, which are often found in the kidney next to the tumor. About 5 to 10% of tumors are bilateral, either at the same time or in sequence, and bilateral disease suggests a germline predisposition.
Morphology: a tumor that copies nephrogenesis

Grossly the tumor is large, solitary, well circumscribed, soft, and tan to gray, with areas of hemorrhage and necrosis. The classic triphasic histology recapitulates kidney development: sheets of small round blue blastemal cells, a fibroblastic or myxoid stroma that may contain skeletal muscle, and an epithelial component forming abortive tubules and glomeruli. Diffuse anaplasia, with large bizarre nuclei and abnormal mitoses, is linked to TP53 mutation and a worse prognosis.
Genetics and associated syndromes

WT1 on chromosome 11p13 encodes a zinc finger transcription factor needed for normal development of the kidney and gonads and later expressed in podocytes. Its loss explains why Wilms tumor risk travels with genitourinary malformations. A second locus, WT2 at 11p15.5, is an imprinted region: IGF2 is normally expressed only from the paternal allele, and loss of imprinting or paternal uniparental disomy gives two active copies, which drives overgrowth and tumor risk. Most sporadic Wilms tumors lack WT1 mutations; activating beta-catenin (CTNNB1) mutations are found in a minority.

blocks.title: Syndromes that predispose to Wilms tumor
rows: Germline deletion at 11p13 removing WT1 and PAX6
Aniridia, genitourinary anomalies (cryptorchidism, hypospadias), intellectual disability
Adjacent PAX6 loss adds aniridia; about one third develop Wilms tumor
Dominant negative missense mutation in the WT1 DNA-binding zinc finger
Early nephrotic syndrome (diffuse mesangial sclerosis), gonadal dysgenesis, often 46,XY with ambiguous genitalia
Mutant protein blocks normal WT1; risk about 90%
Imprinting defects at 11p15.5 (WT2 region), including biallelic IGF2 expression
Macroglossia, organomegaly, hemihyperplasia, omphalocele, neonatal hypoglycemia from islet hyperplasia, adrenal cytomegaly
IGF2 excess drives overgrowth; hepatoblastoma risk too
blocks.caption: WT1 lesions link the tumor to genitourinary and podocyte abnormalities; 11p15.5 lesions link it to overgrowth.

blocks.text: Presentation

The typical child presents with a large, smooth, unilateral flank or abdominal mass, often noticed by a parent while bathing or dressing the child, that usually does not cross the midline. Hematuria occurs when the tumor invades the collecting system, and abdominal pain may follow hemorrhage into the tumor. Hypertension results from renin secreted by the tumor or from compression of renal vessels that makes the kidney ischemic and releases renin. Hematogenous spread goes mainly to the lungs.

blocks.title: Wilms tumor versus neuroblastoma
rows: Neural crest cells of the adrenal medulla or sympathetic ganglia
Smooth, usually does not cross the midline
Irregular, often crosses the midline, often calcified
Raised vanillylmandelic acid and homovanillic acid
Small round blue cells with Homer Wright rosettes
blocks.caption: Both are abdominal masses of young children made partly of small round blue cells; origin and urine markers separate them.

blocks.title: Reasoning from associated anomalies
blocks.text: A 2-year-old with ambiguous genitalia and a 46,XY karyotype has heavy proteinuria, low serum albumin, and a rising creatinine; imaging shows a renal mass. Heavy proteinuria in infancy points to a podocyte disorder, ambiguous genitalia to failed gonadal development, and both require WT1. A dominant negative WT1 mutation explains all three findings, so this is Denys-Drash syndrome, with diffuse mesangial sclerosis and Wilms tumor. With aniridia and developmental delay instead, an 11p13 deletion (WAGR) would fit better.

sections.title: Urothelial carcinoma of the bladder and collecting system

blocks.text: Urothelium lines the renal pelvis, ureters, bladder, and proximal urethra, and urothelial carcinoma can arise anywhere along it, although the bladder is by far the most common site. Urothelial carcinoma accounts for about 90% of bladder cancers. It is about three times more common in men, and most patients are older than 50.
Risk factors and the field effect

The common thread in the risk factors is that a carcinogen or its metabolite is excreted into urine and held against the urothelium during bladder storage. Aromatic amines such as 4-aminobiphenyl and 2-naphthylamine are N-hydroxylated in the liver, conjugated, and excreted; in urine they can be released as reactive species that form DNA adducts in urothelial cells. Because the whole urothelial surface is exposed, mutations accumulate at many sites, so tumors are often multifocal and recur at new locations after removal. Seeding of shed tumor cells into new areas of mucosa contributes as well.

blocks.title: Risk factors for urothelial carcinoma
rows: Most important risk factor; aromatic amines in smoke are excreted in urine; risk several-fold higher
2-naphthylamine and benzidine in aniline dye, rubber, leather, and textile work
Metabolite acrolein is concentrated in urine, causes hemorrhagic cystitis, and raises later cancer risk
Long-term analgesic abuse; linked especially to carcinoma of the renal pelvis, along with analgesic nephropathy
Aristolochic acid and Lynch syndrome (upper tract tumors), arsenic, pelvic radiation
blocks.caption: Each exposure reaches the urothelium through the urine, which is why tumors are multifocal.

blocks.title: Field effect in the urothelium
steps: Stored urine bathes the entire urothelium
DNA damage accumulates at many mucosal sites
Multifocal tumors that recur at new sites
blocks.caption: A urinary carcinogen exposes the renal pelvis, ureters, and bladder at once.

blocks.text: Two pathways: papillary tumors and flat carcinoma in situ

blocks.title: Papillary urothelial tumors versus flat carcinoma in situ
rows: Flat, red, velvety mucosa, sometimes invisible on cystoscopy
Low grade tumors recur often but seldom invade; high grade ones can invade
High risk of progression to invasive carcinoma
Usually positive (cells are poorly cohesive and shed)
blocks.caption: The flat lesion looks less dramatic but is the more dangerous one.

blocks.text: Deletions on chromosome 9, including CDKN2A, are common in both pathways. Prognosis depends mainly on depth of invasion, and invasion of the muscularis propria (detrusor) is the key threshold. Urothelial papilloma (benign) and papillary urothelial neoplasm of low malignant potential sit at the low end of the papillary spectrum.
Manifestations

The classic presentation is painless gross hematuria in an older adult, because fragile vessels in papillary fronds and the friable mucosa of CIS bleed easily. Bleeding is often intermittent, so one normal urinalysis does not exclude a tumor. Carcinoma in situ irritates the bladder and can cause dysuria, frequency, and urgency without infection. A tumor at a ureteral orifice or in the renal pelvis or ureter obstructs urine flow and causes hydronephrosis and flank pain.

blocks.predict: An older smoker with intermittent painless gross hematuria has negative urine cytology. Why does this not rule out urothelial carcinoma?
blocks.explain: Low grade papillary tumors are made of cohesive, near-normal cells that shed poorly and look bland, so cytology is often negative. Cytology is most sensitive for high grade lesions such as CIS.

sections.title: Squamous cell carcinoma and adenocarcinoma of the bladder

blocks.text: Under chronic injury, urothelium can change into another epithelial type. Squamous metaplasia replaces it with keratinizing stratified squamous epithelium, and glandular metaplasia (cystitis glandularis) replaces it with columnar or intestinal-type epithelium. Each metaplastic epithelium can progress through dysplasia to a carcinoma of its own type, which is why the cause of the injury predicts the histology.
Squamous cell carcinoma and Schistosoma haematobium

Squamous cell carcinoma makes up only a few percent of bladder cancers in North America and Europe but is much more frequent where Schistosoma haematobium is endemic, in parts of Africa and the Middle East. This trematode enters through the skin from fresh water, and the adult worms live in the venous plexus around the bladder. They release eggs with a terminal spine that must cross the bladder wall to leave in urine. Many eggs remain trapped and provoke granulomatous inflammation with eosinophils, followed by fibrosis and calcification of the wall, with hematuria from the start. Years of inflammation, cell turnover, reactive oxygen species from inflammatory cells, and N-nitroso compounds formed during bacterial superinfection drive squamous metaplasia, dysplasia, and keratinizing squamous cell carcinoma.

blocks.title: Schistosomal squamous cell carcinoma
steps: S. haematobium eggs lodge in the bladder wall
Fibrosis and calcification with ongoing urothelial injury
blocks.caption: Chronic inflammation, not the parasite's genes, drives the change; the same sequence follows other chronic irritants.

blocks.text: Other sources of chronic irritation follow the same path: long-term indwelling catheters, bladder stones, and recurrent infection in a neurogenic bladder after spinal cord injury. Smoking also contributes. Squamous tumors tend to be found at an advanced stage, and keratin pearls and intercellular bridges identify them microscopically.
Adenocarcinoma: urachal remnants and exstrophy

Primary adenocarcinoma is uncommon, about 2% or less of bladder cancers. In the fetus the urachus, the remnant of the allantois, connects the bladder dome to the umbilicus and normally becomes the fibrous median umbilical ligament. When part of its lumen persists, its glandular epithelium can give rise to urachal adenocarcinoma at the dome or anterior wall, which may grow into the space of Retzius and may secrete mucin into the urine. Bladder exstrophy is a ventral body wall defect: the body wall below the umbilicus fails to close, so the bladder mucosa lies open on the abdomen. Chronic exposure and infection cause glandular metaplasia, and the risk of adenocarcinoma rises.

blocks.title: Bladder carcinomas by histologic type
rows: A few percent (much higher in endemic schistosomiasis)
S. haematobium, catheters, stones, neurogenic bladder
Dome location for urachal tumors; mucin
blocks.caption: The type of chronic injury predicts the type of carcinoma.

integration.text: Each tumor in this chapter is explained by joining a cell of origin to a genetic lesion. Embryology and histology supply the cell: proximal tubule for clear cell and papillary carcinoma, intercalated cell for chromophobe carcinoma and oncocytoma, metanephric blastema for Wilms tumor, and urothelium, its metaplastic variants, or the urachus for bladder tumors. Biochemistry and genetics supply the driver: VHL loss and pseudohypoxic HIF signaling, MET activation, WT1 loss and IGF2 imprinting, and FGFR3 versus TP53 pathways. Physiology then explains the presentations, since a tumor of renal epithelium can make erythropoietin and renin, and gross anatomy explains the left varicocele and the venous route to the lung.

Microbiology and immunology enter through Schistosoma haematobium, where Th2-driven granulomas and years of inflammation, rather than the parasite's own genes, produce squamous cancer. The associations in this chapter are probabilities, not rules: smoking raises the risk of both renal and urothelial carcinoma, a single renal mass may be benign, and histologic overlap between eosinophilic tumors means morphology must be read with genetics and the gross appearance.

summary: Clear cell RCC arises from the proximal tubule; biallelic VHL loss on 3p stabilizes HIF and causes VEGF-driven hypervascularity and erythropoietin secretion.
Clear cell RCC is golden yellow because its cells store lipid, and it grows into the renal vein and inferior vena cava, so metastases go most often to lung, then bone.
Smoking is the strongest modifiable risk factor for both RCC and urothelial carcinoma; obesity, hypertension, dialysis-related cysts, and VHL disease add RCC risk.

RCC classically presents with hematuria, and less often with the full triad; paraneoplastic erythropoietin, PTHrP, renin, and ACTH explain polycythemia, hypercalcemia, hypertension, and Cushing syndrome.
A left varicocele that persists when supine suggests left renal vein obstruction because the left gonadal vein drains into the left renal vein.
Papillary RCC (trisomy 7 and 17, MET, foamy macrophages) shares a proximal tubule origin with clear cell RCC; chromophobe RCC and benign oncocytoma both arise from intercalated cells.

Wilms tumor of children aged 2 to 5 years is a large unilateral flank mass with triphasic histology; WT1 at 11p13 links it to WAGR and Denys-Drash, and 11p15.5 imprinting links it to Beckwith-Wiedemann.

Urothelial carcinoma presents with painless hematuria and is multifocal because urinary carcinogens bathe the whole urothelium; low grade papillary tumors recur, while flat CIS is high grade and often progresses to invasion.
Chronic irritation leads to metaplasia: Schistosoma haematobium and catheters cause squamous cell carcinoma, and urachal remnants and exstrophy cause adenocarcinoma.

The competency lists acquired cystic disease as a clear cell RCC risk factor; Robbins describes papillary carcinoma as the most common type in dialysis-associated cystic disease. This chapter presents it as a risk factor for RCC in general; confirm the framing NABNE uses.
Papillary RCC origin: proximal tubule here; some older Robbins editions say distal convoluted tubule.
Wilms tumor risk figures for WAGR (about one third) and Denys-Drash (about 90%) and the bilateral rate (about 5 to 10%) are approximate consensus values.
Bladder cancer proportions (urothelial about 90%, squamous a few percent outside endemic regions, adenocarcinoma about 2% or less) differ slightly between texts and regions.
The exact chapter title for Schistosoma in the current Jawetz edition should be confirmed.

Birt-Hogg-Dube syndrome, Lynch syndrome, and aristolochic acid are USMLE-level extensions beyond the listed NPLEX conditions (renal cell carcinoma and Wilms tumor); bladder tumors (UR-12-G.5 and G.6) are USMLE extension content. Confirm coverage depth.
Exstrophy mechanism: Langman cites failed lateral body wall fold closure; older texts cite failed mesoderm migration.
